title: AI needs trust – and Australia can provide the verification
gist: Because competitive pressure prevents unilateral AI slowdowns, pacing frontier AI requires an international agreement whose viability hinges on verification — as with Cold War nuclear arms control. The author argues Australia, with no frontier labs, 21 CTBT monitoring stations, ASNO, a new AI Safety Institute and 160 data centres, should fund an AI verification research program including power-monitoring to detect banned training runs.

themes.theme: Verification as the bottleneck for AI arms control

insights.claim: Competitive pressure makes it hard for any frontier lab or nation to slow AI development unilaterally, so any slowdown must be coordinated and codified in an international agreement pacing frontier AI.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Absent a treaty, the frontier AI race — and associated capex — continues unabated.
insights.locator: Competitive pressures in the AI race

insights.claim: The main obstacle to an AI pacing agreement is verifying compliance; without it, each signatory is incentivised to assume others cheat and cheat in turn — the same central problem as Cold War nuclear arms control.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Verification technology is a prerequisite for any binding AI governance regime.
insights.quote: Without the ability to verify compliance, each signatory is incentivised to assume the worst of others and cheat in turn.

insights.claim: An AI agreement might cap the compute spent on training new models, with verification letting all signatories confirm no one exceeded the cap.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Compute caps would directly affect demand for AI training hardware and data-centre capacity.
insights.locator: Australia should invest in the capability

insights.claim: Verification techniques will not by themselves create US and Chinese political will to agree on pacing frontier AI, but credible, scalable methods make such agreements easier.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: No near-term AI treaty is implied; this is a long-term capability build.

insights.claim: Australia's lack of frontier AI models is an advantage for verification: a verifier hosting frontier labs is less trusted because it could go easy on its own labs or spy on rivals' methods.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Middle powers without frontier labs could carve out influential roles in AI governance.
insights.locator: Australia is particularly well-placed to lead

insights.claim: Australia's US alliance means Beijing will not see it as neutral, but its few conflicts of interest still make it a credible contributor to a multilateral verification body.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Limits Australia's role to multilateral contributor rather than sole arbiter.

insights.claim: In 1996 Australia broke a consensus stalemate on the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty by taking the draft directly to the UN General Assembly, showing a state without nuclear weapons can lead.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for middle-power leadership in technology arms control.
insights.quote: In the same way that a state without nuclear weapons rescued the test ban, states without frontier labs can be political leaders in AI verification.
insights.locator: It has also done this before

insights.claim: Australia hosts 21 International Monitoring System facilities — the third most of any country — covering the Indian Ocean, Southern Ocean, Pacific approaches and Antarctic territory, an investment that has paid dividends in technical capability and political standing.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Existing monitoring infrastructure is a base for extending verification expertise to AI.
insights.locator: It has also done this before

insights.claim: The Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office (ASNO) already regulates nuclear and chemical test-ban obligations and researches verification with universities, CSIRO and ANSTO, so AI verification know-how need not be reinvented.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
entities: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation
Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation
insights.so_what: Australia has transferable bureaucratic capacity for AI verification.
insights.locator: Verification institutions already exist in Canberra

insights.claim: Australia's AI Safety Institute, announced December 2025 with $29.9 million over four years, is advisory with no AI-specific regulation; an MOU commits Anthropic to joint safety evaluations with AISI alongside US, UK and Japanese institutes.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Australia's AI-governance institutions are small but linked to frontier labs and peer institutes.

insights.claim: ASNO covers nuclear and chemical verification while AISI has no explicit verification mandate, and nothing joins the two — that gap is where AI verification capability should sit.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific institutional gap a government program could fill.

insights.claim: Australia hosts 160 data centres with 90 more in development, providing real operating conditions for testing verification methods.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Australia's data-centre build-out could double as a verification-research platform.
insights.locator: The hardware is in Australia, too

insights.claim: Early results suggest electricity-use patterns can distinguish AI training from other computation, offering a possible way to check whether a data centre ran training banned by an agreement.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Power-monitoring could become a compliance tool affecting data-centre operators and grid metering.
insights.locator: The hardware is in Australia, too

insights.claim: Canberra should fund a dedicated AI verification research program jointly scoped by ASNO and AISI, open to universities, start-ups and data-centre operators, and support voluntary pilots installing verification instrumentation in new facilities.
insights.speaker: Tom Kimpson
insights.so_what: Potential new funding stream and regulatory instrumentation requirements for Australian data-centre operators.
